original_question: Does there exist a totally ordered group in which all strictly positive elements are conjugate?
target_in_paper: Section 3, Problem 3.31 (listed among the new problems): "Does there exist a totally ordered group all of whose strictly positive elements are conjugate?" ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.2621.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already identifies the exact problem targeted in the paper, with essentially the same wording and scope: an existence question about a totally ordered group whose strictly positive elements are all mutually conjugate. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.2621.pdf))
missing_details: In the paper's Section 3 context, a "totally ordered group" means an ordered group (an o-group): a group equipped with a total order that is preserved by multiplication on both the left and the right. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.2621.pdf))

The order is part of the structure being sought; the question is not merely whether an abstract group is orderable, but whether there exists a specific bi-invariant total order with the stated conjugacy property. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.2621.pdf))
The phrase "strictly positive" should be made explicit as meaning elements g with 1 < g relative to the chosen total order. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.2621.pdf))
The conjugacy condition is pairwise: for any two strictly positive elements g and h, there should exist x in the group such that x^-1 g x = h. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.2621.pdf))
refined_question: Does there exist a group G together with a total order <= that is invariant under both left and right multiplication such that, for every g, h in G with 1 < g and 1 < h, there exists x in G satisfying x^-1 g x = h?
justification: The draft is already almost a verbatim restatement of Problem 3.31 in Section 3, so the faithful refinement is only to unpack the paper's implicit terminology: Section 3 treats totally ordered groups as ordered groups with a two-sided invariant total order, and the positivity condition is with respect to that chosen order. The paper does not give an explicit equivalent reformulation of Problem 3.31, but it does record the nearby consequence that a positive answer would imply positive answers to Problems 3.16 and 3.30, which helps confirm that this is the exact narrow target rather than a broader neighboring question. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.2621.pdf))
